name: Luxury Goods
one_liner: High-end fashion, leather goods, jewelry, watches, and accessories whose economics rest on scarcity, brand heritage, and pricing power far above production cost.
how_it_makes_money: Luxury houses sell at very high markups through tightly controlled directly operated stores, e-commerce, and selective wholesale. Pricing power, brand desirability, and control of distribution let leaders raise prices regularly without losing core demand.
revenue_formula: Revenue = number of boutiques × sales per boutique (clients × transactions × average ticket)
Revenue growth = price increases + volume + mix (leather goods, jewelry, ready-to-wear)
Revenue = top clients (VICs) × spend per client + aspirational buyers × spend
cost_structure: Retail network: prime-location boutique rents and staff
Marketing and brand events: runway shows, celebrity partnerships, flagships
Cost of goods: relatively small vs price, focused on materials and craftsmanship
margins: Top houses earn gross margins of roughly 65-80% and operating margins that can exceed 30%, while weaker brands earn far less. Brand desirability, pricing power, and the share of directly operated retail drive the spread.

key_metrics.name: Organic revenue growth
key_metrics.what: Growth excluding currency and acquisitions, showing brand momentum.

key_metrics.name: Like-for-like sales
key_metrics.what: Sales growth in existing stores, a gauge of demand.

key_metrics.name: Price vs volume contribution
key_metrics.what: Whether growth is from price increases or more buyers, important after years of hikes.

key_metrics.name: Retail vs wholesale mix
key_metrics.what: Share of direct sales, linked to brand control and margin.

key_metrics.name: Share of sales from top clients
key_metrics.what: Concentration of revenue in VICs, which shows resilience.
